objective: Control life-threatening external bleeding with direct pressure, a tourniquet or wound packing
secondaryObjectives: Keep a patient in shock warm and positioned, and prepare for a rapid handover
Recognize scene hazards and decide whether to enter, wait or withdraw
Hand over care to the transporting crew with a concise report

sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in ACS's handout (primary): red criteria include active bleeding requiring a tourniquet or wound packing with continuous pressure, SBP < 90 or HR > SBP at age 10-64, motor GCS < 6, RR < 10 or > 29, room-air SpO2 < 90%; any red criterion: the highest-level trauma center available in the regional system; yellow (mechanism such as rider separated from a vehicle with significant impact): a trauma center, not necessarily the highest level.

sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in a text extraction of the Louisiana copy (the extractor did not keep every table column, so placement was checked against the course's own reading of 2026-11-09 in ems-sources.ts). EMR: CPR and AED, tourniquet and wound packing, naloxone, oral airway, BVM, oxygen; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector, aspirin, oral glucose, CPAP, 12-lead acquisition (not interpretation), transport. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways and a limited list of IV and IM medications including dextrose and glucagon. Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, intubation and the wider formulary. No newer model was found 2026-11-11 (EMS.gov's page was unavailable; the only other 'update' found is the 2017 change notice adding tourniquets, wound packing and naloxone to EMR and EMT).

brief.situation: 15:10. You are an EMR in a quick-response vehicle, first on scene at a cabinet shop. A board kicked back off the table saw and gashed a 34-year-old man's left thigh, mid-thigh on the front. He is sitting on the floor next to the saw, pressing the wound with both hands; bright red blood is pulsing between his fingers.
handover: A coworker called 911 and is standing by, shaken but willing to help. A BLS ambulance is about 10 minutes out.
Your kit: gloves and eye protection, gauze, pressure bandages, two commercial tourniquets, a marker, blankets. You can take a manual blood pressure, pulse and breathing rate.
As an EMR you do not transport and give no IV fluids: stop the bleeding, treat for shock, and hand over.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Blood loss keeps adding up until the bleeding is controlled. Your hands can do one thing at a time; give the coworker clear jobs.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when the ambulance crew takes over, then a debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why a tourniquet here rather than a bigger dressing, and how did you place and check it?

parts.label: Choosing the tourniquet
parts.criteria: Pulsing bright red bleeding from a limb is life-threatening; direct pressure first and at once, then a commercial tourniquet when pressure does not control it; a pressure dressing soaks through and wastes time.
parts.modelAnswer: Bright red, pulsing blood from the thigh is arterial and life-threatening. Press hard at once, then put on a tourniquet because pressure alone did not stop it. A pressure bandage just soaks through.

parts.label: Placement and checks
parts.criteria: 2-3 inches above the wound, not over a joint, tightened until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone; a second above the first if it still bleeds; time written; not loosened for pain; then flat, warm, nothing by mouth.
parts.modelAnswer: On the thigh 2-3 inches above the wound, not over the knee, tightened until the bleeding stops and the foot pulse is gone; a second one above it when it still oozed. Time written on it, left in view, never loosened for pain. Then flat, warm, nothing to drink.

noProgress.rationale: A crew arriving to a limb still bleeding after 7-10 minutes means the treatment that saves this patient was never completed; this case calls it harm.

expertPath.text: Saw off at the wall, gloves and glasses on, kneel beside him. Hard direct pressure with gauze at once.
Coworker takes over the pressure; tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound, tightened until the pulsing stops and the foot pulse is gone.
Still oozing: second tourniquet above the first. Time written, left uncovered. Radio for paramedics.
Flat, blankets, nothing by mouth. Vital signs. He asks you to loosen it: no.
Hand over: tourniquet time, second tourniquet, estimated loss, vital-sign trend.

collapse.headline: He bled into class IV shock
collapse.body: Pulsing bleeding from the thigh can empty a patient in minutes. Look at how long the wound went without firm pressure and how long until a correctly placed tourniquet.

stillBleeding.headline: Still bleeding when the crew came
stillBleeding.body: A pressure bandage soaks through, and a tourniquet over or below the wound, or only snug, cannot stop arterial flow. Above the wound, tight until the bleeding and the distal pulse stop, a second if needed.

controlledHandoff.headline: Bleeding stopped early, clean handoff
controlledHandoff.body: Safe scene, pressure at once, a correct tourniquet within seconds and a second when it oozed, time written, shock care and a complete report: the expert path.

controlledGaps.headline: Stopped, with gaps
controlledGaps.body: The bleeding stopped, but check the timeline: the running saw, gloves, the delay before control, a loosened tourniquet, or a report without the tourniquet time.

time_up.headline: No handover
time_up.body: Twenty minutes passed without a handover.

scoring.modelReasoning: Make the scene safe first (switch the saw off, gloves and eye protection). Bright red pulsing blood from the thigh is life-threatening: press hard at once, hand the pressure to a helper, and apply a commercial tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound, not over a joint, tightened until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. If it still oozes, a second tourniquet above the first. Write the time on it, leave it uncovered, never loosen it for pain. Then treat for shock: flat, warm, nothing by mouth. Ask for paramedics (a tourniquet is a red field-triage criterion) and hand over with the tourniquet time, the estimated loss and the vital-sign trend.

pulse.ask: While you turn the windlass: how will you know it is tight enough?

choices.label: The bleeding stops and the pulse below it is gone
The skin under it turns white

pulse.explain: Tighten until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. Pain is expected and is not the end point; a tourniquet only snug blocks the veins and makes bleeding worse.

crewWait.ask: While the ambulance comes: he begs you to loosen it because it hurts. What do you do?

choices.label: Leave it tight, explain why, and tell the crew he needs pain relief
Loosen it a little every few minutes
Take it off now the bleeding has stopped

crewWait.explain: Never loosen a tourniquet to relieve pain; pain is treated with analgesics by the transporting crew. Loosening restarts the bleeding.
